utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case next on the list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-30/1-A, the Prosecutor versus Miroslav Kvocka, Mladjo Radic, Zoran Zigic, and Dragoljub Prcac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I must, in the usual way, test the equipment. So, ladies and gentlemen, can you hear me? Firstly, interpreters? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The appellants. How will we do that? Mr. Simic, you first. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Your colleagues. Yes, they hear me. In the Prosecution? Yes. Yes. Now, the appearances for the parties. Will you please tell me who is appearing for whom. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning. My name is Krstan Simic. I'm appearing on behalf of Miroslav Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Toma Fila, defending Mladjo Radic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We're not getting the interpretation--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear interpreting into English? Is there anything on channel 4?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. And the third gentleman. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Jovan Simic, attorney-at-law, appearing for Dragoljub Prcac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning. My name is Slobodan Stojanovic, attorney-at-law from Belgrade, appearing for the accused Zoran Zigic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Good. Thank you very much. And now for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Anthony Carmona, and I appear on behalf of the Prosecution. Appearing on the Prosecution -- with me is Ms. Norul Rashid, Ms. Helen Brady, Ms. Kelly Howick, and Mr. David Re. Mr. David Re will be conducting the examination of the particular witness on behalf of the Prosecution. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, good. I propose now to make a brief introductory statement before we proceed with the hearing of the witness in this case. The case before us today is Prosecutor against Miroslav Kvocka, Mladjo Radic, Zoran Zigic, and Dragoljub Prcac. The case at first instance had five co-accused persons. All five were convicted at the close of the trial on 2nd November 2001. One of those convicted, namely, Mr. Kos, filed his notice of appeal on 16th November 2001, but he withdrew it on 21st May 2002, and he was subsequently released by the Tribunal. Now, the Trial Chamber convicted each of the appellants of persecution, murder, and torture, and also the Appellant Zigic of cruel treatment as well. These crimes are recognised in Articles 3 and 5 of the Statute. The appellants filed notices of appeal between 13 and 16 November 2001. The Prosecution did not appeal. Now, during the appellate proceedings, four motions were filed pursuant to Rule 115 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, seeking to admit additional evidence on appeal. The Appellant Prcac filed his Rule 115 motion on 25 February 2003, with an addendum on 10th March 2003. The Appellant Radic filed his Rule 115 motion on 25 February 2003, and an addendum on 2nd March 2003. The Appellant Zigic filed his first Rule 115 motion on 22 August 2002, with an addendum on 13 June 2003. He filed a second Rule 115 motion on 11th April 2003, with a supplement on 19th May 2003. On 16 February 2004, that is, last month, the Appeals Chamber issued a decision on the Rule 115 motions. It granted only in part the motions filed by the Appellant Zigic, while it dismissed the rest of the submissions by the appellants. Two additional witnesses were ordered by the Appeals Chamber, under Rules 98 and 107 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal. They were ordered to appear on the hearing in this appeal scheduled on that day for 23rd March 2004. The Scheduling Order which prescribed that also ordered the Prosecution to file any rebuttal material by 27 February 2004, and the appellant to file -- the appellant to respond to such material by 5 March 2004, and the Prosecution to reply by 10 March 2004. The Prosecution filed its rebuttal material on 27 February 2004. The Appellant Zigic responded on 8 March 2004. Then the Prosecution replied on 11 March 2004. By decision of 12 March 2004, both the Appellant Zigic and the Prosecution were granted extensions of time for the respective filings. The decision of 12 March 2004 also found admissible as rebuttal material the evidence contained in the witness statements submitted by the Prosecution. Now, by order of 26th February 2004, Appeals Chamber directed the Victims and Witness Section to make arrangements for the additional witnesses to appear before the Appeals Chamber today, on 23rd March 2004. According to their information, Witness KV1, that is, one of the two witnesses, was willing to come to testify before the Appeals Chamber, but the other witness was reluctant to do so. A subpoena was issued on 11 March 2004 to the second witness. Despite the efforts of the Chamber, it has not been able to secure his appearance today. However, the Appeals Chamber will take appropriate steps to arrange for his testimony to be given, if possible, after the hearings for this week. As the rebuttal evidence is concerned only with the additional evidence to be given by the second additional witness, we will not have any rebuttal witnesses today, but we will have them at a later stage, if and when we can secure the appearance of the second additional witness. For today's evidentiary hearing, there is, therefore, only Witness KV1 to be heard by this Chamber. Pursuant to the Scheduling Order of 19 March 2004, as amended by the Scheduling Order of 22 March 2004, the Appeals Chamber will first direct questions to Witness KV1. Following the questioning by the Chamber, the Appellant Zigic and the Prosecution will have 30 minutes to examine the witness. Of course, the Judges will also ask questions. The Appellant Zigic and the Prosecution are reminded that this is not a new trial. Further, I would remind them that they will be given an opportunity to present arguments on the weight and credibility of the evidence given today by Witness KV1 in the course of their final arguments. Finally, the parties are reminded that they are not allowed to contact the witness out of court at any time during his testimony. Unless there are any questions, we will now proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, could you please read the solemn declaration which will be given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down. Now, I should explain that by order dated 18th March 2004, this witness was granted the pseudonym of KV1, as well as facial distortion. I would remind all parties to use this pseudonym at all times during this hearing, and since I'm prone, first of all, to forget that Rule, I remind myself also of it. If there is any accident, then the registrar will please draw that to our notice so that we may make an immediate correction of the text. Well, now, Madam Registrar, will you please show the witness his name and his date of birth on a piece of paper. I believe you have already shown it to the parties.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We are concerned to protect your identity, and therefore, we will refer to you throughout as Witness KV1. Now, I will begin the questioning. My colleagues on the Bench will join in, and the parties will also ask you questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, you are from where, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I am from Prijedor. I was born in Kljuc, but I lived in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, did you know a man by the name of Drago Tokmandzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Do you mean Drago Tokmandzic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That's correct. Do forgive me for my execrable pronunciation. It is to that gentleman that I'm referring. Is he still alive or has he passed away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: He has passed away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, we want you to help us to understand the circumstances in which he passed away. Can you remember when, about when he passed away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date, but I know that he died in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Keraterm was what at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: It was a camp in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Were you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: As what were you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I was a detainee, a prisoner there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And you arrived there when? Can you tell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: On 31st of May, or was it April? I'm not quite sure any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And when, or about when, did you leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: On the 5th of August, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, where did you stay in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: At the outset, I was in room number 2, then in room number 1, and then I spent the bulk of my time in room number 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Could you help us to understand how the rooms were situated. Were there a number of rooms in the same building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: There were four rooms.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, you told us where you were. And where was Tokmadzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Mr. Tokmadzic, when he was brought there, was immediately put in room number 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, you said, I think, that you remembered his passing away. Could you tell the Chamber what you recall about that, in your own words.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: That evening, Banovic, together with Keli - I know that - called out Tokmadzic's name, Islamovic, Kljaic, Mesic. I can't remember all of those whose names were called out, but I know there were quite a few of them. They were taken outside. They were beaten up. After some time, some of them were brought back. Drago Tokmadzic was already dead when they threw him back into the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, from where you were in your room, to where this beating happened, could you tell us what the distance was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: A few metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you hear any voices during the beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Were you able to identify these voices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes. That of Banovic and Keli. I'm sure I also heard Goran Lajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you hear any other voices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: There were many sounds, and there may have been some that I didn't register. But I did register the ones that were familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, did you hear any reference to a pig? Did anybody use the word "pig"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did anybody use the words "finish him off"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you see a man called Edin Ganic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Was he a prisoner in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I can't recall, but I'm sure he wasn't in my room, number 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, in your room, there were some other people. Were there some people from Puharska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I may not be pronouncing the word correctly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there were. Most of them were from Puharska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, did you hear a vehicle arriving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: No, although vehicles did frequently arrive, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you hear these people from Puharska saying anything about who was coming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: The only thing I remember is I know that when Kajin arrived, then the beatings would stop. He probably didn't permit that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, I would invite you to look at a piece of paper. It has a name on it. That is a name of a protected witness. I just want you to look at the paper and to tell the Court if you knew that this man was also a prisoner in the camp. Don't call his name, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I remember the last name. I'm not sure about his first name, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Will the usher please show the gentlemen at the bar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes, he was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So you say that Witness Y was also a prisoner in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I'm not saying precisely that he was in that room. I know there was someone of that last name there, but I cannot confirm the first name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Thank you. Now, one last question, or set of questions. Did you know a man by the name of Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, did you see him during your stay in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you see him at the time when Tokmadzic was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I really didn't see him on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: If you saw him now, would you recognise him? I'm talking about Mr. Zigic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Have you seen him recently anywhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Well, not until just a little while ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So you saw him a little while ago. Where is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Here, to my left side, in the first row, between those two policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. My colleagues will ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Just a couple of clarifications, Witness KV1. In answering to the Presiding Judge, you said that when the beating of Mr. Tokmadzic occurred, you heard a number of voices. Among them, you mentioned the voice of Mr. Lajic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us whether, from the voice, from his voice, you can assess that he was actually beating Mr. Tokmadzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I don't know who was beating who that night, but I did hear his voice. There were several people outside who were beaten up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So you cannot say whether he personally was beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. That's all I wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Guney. Judge Guney will ask some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you've spoke of many beatings, and you heard in the course the voice of Ganic. Could you tell us: What was the role played by Mr. Ganic, if you could make it out, of course, in those beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I spoke about Goran Lajic, that I heard his voice, not the voice of Ganic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But given that you've just told us that you had known him for a period of time - I'm talking of Zoran Zigic - did you hear the voice of Mr. Zoran Zigic in the course of the beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In what state was the corpse of Mr. Tokmadzic when it was thrown into your room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: He was dead. It was dark. We couldn't really get a good look at him. But I do know that he was dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you notice traces of torture, beatings, even if it was dark?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Not at that time. We couldn't see anything. We just realised that he wasn't breathing, that he was no longer living. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness KV1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Weinberg de Roca will ask some questions now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a few questions. Who called on that -- the detainees that were then later beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Banovic and Keli.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA
utterances.text: Did you -- how many people were called?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact number. There were quite a few of them. I know that Tokmadzic and Eso -- the policeman who was brought in with him, and Lajic and Mesic, and an Albanian. Their names were called out. The Albanian died seven days later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA
utterances.text: And do you know how many people were beating these detainees, or did you only hear the voices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I don't know how many people were beating the prisoners, but I heard the voices that I was able to recognise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA
utterances.text: You recognised all the voices, or only some of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I recognised only those three voices that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA
utterances.text: But were there or -- were there more people beating the detainees, and you recognised three voices, or do you think it was only those three that were beating the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I think there were more people beating the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA
utterances.text: Did you recognise voices and sounds or did you also recognise what was being said, or was it just the sound you heard but not the exact words?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I couldn't repeat the exact words. They were curses and cries like "hit him," and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Though this witness is a witness of the Appeals Chamber, the witness has really been called at the request of Mr. Zigic. So would counsel for Mr. Zigic wish to ask any questions at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I am grateful that after this exhaustive questioning by the Trial Chamber, I have only a few questions left to put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. KV1. There is only one detail I would like to clarify. Do you remember how Drago Tokmadzic was dressed in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: He was wearing a light-blue police shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he brought in wearing that shirt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this, in fact, the police uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this the kind of uniform then also worn by members of the Serb police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: This was the uniform of the police of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, the part of the police we might term the Serb police, after the well-known events in Prijedor, did the policemen who remained in the service of the Serbian authorities there wear the same uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Counsel. May I turn to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I turn to the Prosecution now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness, this room that you were in, room 4, on that particular night, how many people do you estimate were in that room on that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: On that night, there were between 260 and 280.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there a door from that room which went directly out onto the outside area of the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of door was it? Was it a door with grills on it, an open door you could see through, or a closed door?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: It was a metal door, and you could see what was directly in front of the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were you in relation to that door when you heard the sounds of beating outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I was beside the door. There was a little wall there on both sides of the entrance to the room. I was next to the wall that is closer to room number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many people do you estimate were between you and the door?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Between me and the door, there were some 10 or 15 or perhaps even 20 people. Some of them were right next to the door itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And there were also windows to the outside, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you able to see out that night to where the beating was occurring, from where you were inside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: No. The windows were very high up, so you couldn't see out of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there was a barrel containing water outside, near room 4, near the door to room 4?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: There were two barrels.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they contain water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would it be accurate to say that they contained maybe 50 to 100 litres of water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Two barrels of 200 litres each.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did the guards use these barrels of water outside the door to assault or torture the prisoners or detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember, on the night in which Drago Tokmadzic was called out, hearing the sounds of splashing or people using those barrels of water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The place from where you heard the sounds of beating outside the door, do you think it was on the grass or the concrete?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: The place where the beatings happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Where you heard Drago Tokmadzic being beaten. Do you think it was on the grass or the concrete, based upon the sounds you heard and the distance between the door and the concrete?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I can't say whether he was beaten on the grass or on the concrete, because both the grass and the concrete were very close by. There were many voices, moans, a lot of noise, and you couldn't really gather something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And was it apparent to you that more than one person was being beaten outside the door, from the sounds you heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In response to a question from Judge Weinberg de Roca, you mentioned a person called Eso in that room. Was that Esad Islamovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he survive that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there a person in the room or at the camp you knew called Jovo, Jovo Radocac or Radocaj? Forgive my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: After this beating he was thrown into the room. He was stabbed with a knife. He died a little later inside the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll just take you back a step. Firstly, the person Jovo, Jovo -- was it R-a-d-o-c, with an accent, a-j? Is that the spelling of his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said after the beating, he was thrown in the room and he had -- or the translation says he was stabbed with a knife. I'll take you back. Was he one of the people called out from your room, or was he in another room that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: He was not in the room. He wasn't in any of the rooms, actually. I think that on that occasion, he had been brought from elsewhere, from some house, say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And just to clarify your earlier answer about him being stabbed with a knife: Are you saying that he had been stabbed with a knife before he was thrown back into the room, or thrown into the room? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we object. We believe that this examination has gone beyond the scope of what should be the subject matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, the Bench has considered your motion, but refuses it at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was Mr. -- was Jovo thrown back into the room at the same time as Drago Tokmadzic, or at a different time that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: The interval between these two events was short, a couple of minutes, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about times, and I appreciate it's been a very long time. I want you to estimate for the Appeals Chamber, as best as you can, about what time you think Mr. Tokmadzic was called from the room.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: It's very difficult to say. It was night-time. That means after 10.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was he immediately beaten or did you immediately hear the sounds of beating outside your door just after he had been called out by Banovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Not immediately. It took them some time to round up the others and to line them up, and then the whole thing started. How exactly it started, I don't know, but it seems to me that all of them were beating everybody at the same time, and there were several of them involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long did this beating continue for, the one that you could hear outside your window -- or outside the door?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. 10, 15, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could it have been longer than that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Well, to me, it seemed like it was the whole night.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And after the beating, did the voices go away and the sounds subside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes. Everything died down --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And was it --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: -- suddenly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Suddenly. And was it sometime later that Drago Tokmadzic's body was brought back into the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes. After that beating, they threw him inside and in the same way they threw Jovo inside as well, and a bit later, everything was still. Everything was quiet until the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you say whether it was the guards who brought his body back into the room or whether prisoners in the room were asked to go out and bring the body back in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I think two prisoners holding the bodies of Drago Tokmadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying that the guards came and asked the prisoners to come outside and bring the bodies back in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes. They stood in the doorway and asked two men to come out. I think it was the way it happened. It was a long time ago, and I don't have a clear recollection of it any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When Drago Tokmadzic was taken out, you said that you were near the front, I think you said there were a number of people between you and the door, but you were near the wall and the door to the outside. Where were you by the time Drago Tokmadzic was brought back in? Were you still in that spot or had you moved to another one in the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I was in the same spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where or how -- I'm sorry. I withdraw that. Were you one of the people who removed Drago Tokmadzic's body from the room the next day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did you take it to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: He was taken upstairs, above room number 4, to the perimeter, where the waste dump was. There were some pallets there and we laid him on the pallets. I don't remember the other person who was doing the carrying with me. I've already been asked that question, but I can't remember the other man who was carrying the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The translation reads he was taken upstairs, above room 4. Are you saying in the building and into the perimeter of the building, or are you talking about outside somewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: No, no. It was outside. You see, where room 4 is, then after that is the end of the area, the red area, which is fenced in, and then there is an area covered with grass, also fenced in. And we put him outside, on the other side of the fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Approximately how far is that from -- I'm sorry. I withdraw that question. Was that a place where bodies of the deceased prisoners were regularly taken to, that same spot you've just talked about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes, that was the spot. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And approximately how far is that in metres, doing your best, from the door of room 4? 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 100, whatever.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: 30 to 40 metres, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that an area described by the other prisoners as the end of the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would you necessarily have been able to hear the sounds of people at night in that particular area from where you were in room 4?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: From that place, you can hear. It's not far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you heard any sounds coming from that area that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Well, it's not exactly the same spot that you're asking me about now. It's the last room in the row in Keraterm, and we carried the body a bit beyond that room, towards the asphalt road. There is a spot where some pallets are lying, and that's where we put the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How far is that particular place from the door of room 4?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Well, some 40 metres or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would you agree that if you were inside a room with many, many other people, and there were sounds coming from a distance outside, maybe a distance of 30 or 40 metres, it's difficult to identify precisely where the sound is coming from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that this is not only a repetition of a previous question; it is an attempt to confuse the witness, an attempt to replace one thing with another. The witness had described a place just outside room number 4, where Drago Tokmadzic was beaten, and then a completely different place where his body was taken, near a waste dump. The Prosecutor is trying to swap these two places in his examination, and to insinuate that Drago Tokmadzic was beaten in the more distant place, which was 40 metres away from room number 4. It is a different place. The day after, his body was probably taken yet further, to a cemetery, but that's no reason to question this witness about it. I don't think his attempt to confuse the witness is fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The Prosecutor, would you make haste at this point. Mr. Stojanovic's objection takes me to the schedule of our hearings, and you were -- the Prosecution was given 30 minutes. And maybe if you adhered to that timetable, then we wouldn't have any more objections of the nature made by Mr. Stojanovic. Would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I address the objection. I'm putting to this witness the evidence of Witness -- of Edin Ganic. I am -- the Prosecution is not tied to a beating, the death of Mr. Tokmadzic, outside that door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Ganic's evidence is different and I am putting a different scenario to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand, Counsel. What I was reminding you of were the imperatives of the schedule before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked a question about the possibility of this witness being able to identify where sounds are coming from, which is consistent with the evidence heard at trial of Edin Ganic. I didn't get an answer to that question. Twice. I'm trying to get an answer from the question. Can I put the question again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Please proceed quickly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness KV1, did you understand my question? My question is if you are inside a building with many other people present, at night, you would agree that it would be difficult for you to ascertain exactly where sounds are coming from, if they may be coming from a place maybe 30 or 40 metres away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I agree that that is correct, although we were dead silent, all of us in the room. And what I said did not apply to those who were at a distance. It applied to only those that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is: Do you remember on that night hearing sounds that may have been coming from, say, 30 or 40 metres away? The question is: Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I do not remember more remote sounds. I only remember the sounds just outside the room, the racket that was not more than four or five metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you aware of a person -- did you know a person who was a teacher from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I knew a man named Maroslic. Was it Maroslic? I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there a teacher from Kozarac who was also taken out that night and beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: That, I really don't know. But that teacher was in room number 2, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is it possible there was a time period between when the sounds of beating stopped outside your door and Drago Tokmadzic was brought back in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Could you repeat this question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You heard the sounds of beating outside your door, and everything went silent. Was there a time period, a period of time between when the sounds stopped and when he was brought back in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: They brought him back into the room at the very end of this incident, perhaps just moments before everything went silent.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you able to say approximately what time he was brought back in? 10.30, 11.00, 11.30, 12.00, 12.30, 1.00, whatever.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: I already mentioned that I can't tell you exactly how much time passed. To me, it seemed horribly a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want to show you an exhibit from trial. It is Exhibit 327. It is a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown this photograph. I have copies for my colleagues and the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: While it's being done, Witness KV1, you wouldn't have known -- or you wouldn't have been able to see someone being taken out from room 1 from where you were, would you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want you to get a pen and look at that particular exhibit. And I want you to draw an arrow from the sky down to where room 1 was. Can you just turn to your right. Draw an arrow from the top -- from the sky. Can you please draw on it with the pen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you please just mark a "1" above that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you please draw the arrow all the way down to room number 1, to where the door of room number 1 was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to do the same with room number 4, please, that is, an arrow right down to the -- from the sky right down to the door, with a "4" above the top of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Prosecution has available to them much clearer photographs which it has shown to other witnesses. In this photograph, even I, who has visited Keraterm many times, find it difficult to distinguish where room number 4 is. I believe this exhibit was intentionally chosen as one of the least advantageous for identification. I know the Prosecution disposes of many others depicting room 4 much more clearly. I don't know what this is supposed to lead to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, the Bench considers that the point had better be kept by you in reserve for when you address us on the weight of the evidence and on the inferences which could safely be drawn from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll certainly ask my friend to withdraw his insinuation we're choosing exhibits which are least advantageous for identification; this is the best we can find. And he'll do so in his submissions, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please draw a "4" on the line you've drawn on that to show it's room 4.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, I want you to mark an "X" on the spot outside room 4 from where you heard the sounds of beating.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure we can clearly see that "X." Can you make it a little larger, please, or maybe use a different coloured pen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you also put an arrow on that in the direction of the -- pointing in the direction of the garbage dump, the end of the camp, where the bodies were taken to. Well, firstly I should ask you: Can you see that particular spot on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please mark an arrow pointing in the direction of the garbage dump.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And to be clear, you said that was I think 30 or 40 metres from room -- the doorway to room 4.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Might that be received into evidence, please, Your Honours, as an exhibit on appeal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, the first photo will be marked PA1, and the second photo that had been marked by the witness is PA1 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, the Bench will afford you the opportunity to ask any clarifying questions directed to anything new that the Prosecution might have elicited.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe we would only be wasting more time. My objections, however, stand, particularly with regard to the photograph, and I would like to say a few words about that at the end, as you instructed. I have no other questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Gentlemen, I don't -- I think that concludes the examination of the testimony of this witness. If it, pleases you, and there are no serious objections, we think it would be convenient to reserve the addresses of the parties on the evidence for the conclusion of the entire appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We think it may be convenient now to take the adjournment, unless there are any questions from the Bench. There are no questions from the Bench. We will take an adjournment of 30 minutes. We will suspend, and then we will come back for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm reminded by my colleague on my right that the witness might be excused at this point. All right. Well, Judge Guney -- Mr. Usher, will you keep the apparatus on. Judge Guney has a question to ask the witness, and it will be convenient to have this question put before the witness leaves us. Judge Guney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have already asked you a question concerning the corpse of that man. I asked in which state it was, the corpse of Mr. Tokmadzic, when it was brought back to room number 4. And you replied by saying that the lighting was too poor for you to see. And the next day, considering that you were one of the two men who hold the body outside from that room, can you tell me, did you see then in which state the body was. Were there any signs of injuries, torture, beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: There were traces of injuries. We didn't really inspect him carefully. We just had to carry him away, because he was dead. We weren't interested in inspecting his injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And while carrying him, you did not observe nothing beyond what is normal? Nothing struck you in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV1
utterances.text: There were no large wounds on his body. You could see traces of a beating, but I will say again: We didn't really inspect him. We -- it's not a nice thing to look at a dead body, so we averted our gaze as we carried him along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness KV1. It was very good of you to come. Mr. Usher, will you see that the witness takes his leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, we're a few minutes ahead of time, but this might be a convenient stage at which to take the usual break. So I would ask that we suspend the proceedings for 30 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen. I understand from the registrar that there is a technical problem relating to the numbering of two exhibits which were introduced this morning. Madam Registrar, what would you like to do?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to let the parties know the exhibit number and the confidentiality. The first exhibit, it's a Chamber exhibit, which is CA1, is Witness KV1's particulars. This exhibit is under seal. The second Chamber exhibit is CA2, and that is Witness Y's particulars, and that also is under seal. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. If there are no objections, it is so ordered. Then we come now to the hearing of appeals, but I understood that the Prosecution wanted to say a word. Yes, please, Mr. Carmona.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just wish to indicate that in indicating this morning the complement of the Prosecution, I was remiss in not mentioning our diligent case manager, Ms. Lourdes Galicia. And secondly, as a courtesy, I should indicate to the Court, to the learned Chamber, that Mr. David Re, who conducted the examination of the witness, will not be here this afternoon with us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we proceed now with the hearing of the final oral arguments of the parties. I take it that the address system is working and that there's no need to ask whether proceedings are being heard by the interpreters, by the appellants, by the accused, the appellants, or by the Prosecution, and that the appearances now are as they were earlier this morning. Now, the evidential portion of this hearing took place this morning, when one witness testified. I simply confirm that the relevant parties will be at liberty to address the Appeals Chamber on that evidence and its proper evaluation at the relevant time in the course of these arguments. Now, in its judgement rendered on 2nd November 2001, the Trial Chamber convicted the appellants for persecutions, murder, torture, or cruel treatment, all being crimes recognised by Article 3 or Article 5 of the Statute. The Trial Chamber sentenced the Appellant Kvocka to seven years' imprisonment, the Appellant Prcac to five years' imprisonment, the Appellant Radic to 20 years' imprisonment, and the Appellant Zigic to 25 years' imprisonment. The appellants filed their notices of appeal against the trial judgement between the 13th and the 16th of November, 2001. That is a little over three years ago. The Prosecution did not appeal. All four Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. appellants share a common ground of appeal concerning the doctrine of joint criminal enterprise. Their individual grounds of appeal are briefly summarised as follows, and I warn the Bench that I'm not being exhaustive or detailed at this stage. The appellant Mr. Kvocka alleges that the Trial Chamber erred in admitting the transcript of his interviews in finding him to be the deputy commander at Omarska, in finding him to be guilty of persecutions and the crimes of murder and torture, and in ignoring two mitigating factors in determining his sentence. The appellant Mr. Prcac argues that the Trial Chamber should have acquitted him, having accepted his arguments in total; that the Trial Chamber erred in convicting him on the fact that was not pleaded in the indictment and committed errors of fact and law in respect of his role at Omarska; that the Trial Chamber did not explain the credibility of certain witnesses; that the Trial Chamber denied him a fair trial in relation to the cross-examination of ten witnesses; and that the Trial Chamber did not consider certain mitigating facts in determining his sentence. The appellant Mr. Radic alleges that the Trial Chamber denied him a fair trial by failing to assess his responsibility for acts or incidents detailed in the confidential schedules attached to the indictment; that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that he had a discriminatory intent, without proof of it; that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that there was sufficient evidence to corroborate his guilt for maltreatment in the camp; and that the Trial Chamber gave him too severe a sentence, which is disproportionate to his position and inconsistent with the ICTY sentencing practice. The appellant Mr. Zigic contends that the Trial Chamber erred in finding him responsible for murders at the Omarska camp, murders of specific individual detainees, torture, and certain beatings. He submits further that the Trial Chamber erred in relying on evidence of a pattern of conduct which was unfounded; in failing to provide a reasoned opinion for his conviction for persecutions; and in failing to consider mitigating facts in relation to his sentence. He also claims that he was not properly informed of the charges against him and that the Trial Chamber was biased against him in not providing reasons for his convictions. I would now like to remind the parties about the criteria applicable to errors of facts or law alleged on appeal. The Appeals Chamber has pointed out on numerous occasions, an appeal is not an occasion for parties to re-plead their case. It is not a trial de novo. The general rule is that on appeal, the parties must limit their arguments to matters falling within the framework of Article 25 of the Statute, that is, errors and questions of law invalidating the decision or errors of fact which have occasioned a miscarriage of justice. In a rare case, a party may raise an issue of general importance to the Tribunal's jurisprudence. An appellant alleging an error of fact must demonstrate that no reasonable trier of fact could have reached the conclusion being challenged and that this error has caused a miscarriage of justice. The final arguments of the parties will be heard in accordance with the schedule set out in the Scheduling Order of 19th March 2004, as amended by the Scheduling Order of 22 March 2004. At the end of the final arguments, the appellants will be allowed to make brief submissions to the Chamber. Turning now to the Defence for Mr. Prcac, I would invite arguments by him. I will explain that our invitation to counsel for Mr. Prcac to speak first is out of the order indicated in the cover page of the judgement, but that this is due to questions as we perceive them, relating to the need to consolidate the arguments and especially having regard to the necessities of presenting arguments on matters of common concern to the appellants. So would counsel for Mr. Prcac be the first to speak, that is, Mr. Simic. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence of Mr. Prcac submitted this appeal almost two and a half years ago on the grounds that Your Honour has summarised and which we will only briefly discuss. It is -- the standpoint of the Defence has not changed since we submitted our motion. What we put forward, and still argue, is the fact that Mr. Prcac was indicted and charged that, as a deputy commander of the Omarska camp, he held a position which implied his participation in a joint criminal enterprise because the Trial Chamber took the position that the camp itself was a joint criminal enterprise. The indictment that has been confirmed contained assertions by the Prosecution that Mr. Prcac was the deputy commander and that he was superior to everybody in the camp except the commander, that he was able to change the conditions, to make decisions on transferrals of detainees and that he could decide who could enter the Omarska camp and when. These allegations by the Prosecution were rejected by the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber established that Mr. Prcac was not the deputy commander of the camp, that he was not authorised, that he had no authority over the guards and other services in the Omarska camp, that there was a separate chain of command and hierarchy, and that he was not in the position that he -- that the Prosecution claimed he was. However, it was established by the Trial Chamber that he was the administrative assistant of the camp commander. In the view of the Defence, this is not well grounded. But this was used to characterise his position and influence, and the influence that he, as a low-ranking person, could wield on the joint criminal enterprise. This Defence team, as the Appeals Chamber knows, has found it part of its appeal on the standpoints taken by the Trial Chamber in the Krnojelac case, which established some standards which are not new but which the Defence finds acceptable and very efficient in establishing the role, function, and therefore, the criminal responsibility of persons accused as participating in a joint criminal enterprise. This has now entered the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. Participation in a joint criminal enterprise is incorporated in the individual responsibility provided for by Article 7(1) of the Statute of this Tribunal. In the appeals judgement in the Krnojelac case, the Appeals Chamber did not discuss what the Defence thought would be discussed because they presumed the participation of the accused Krnojelac and his position and status in the Foca KP Dom prison, because he was in charge of the functioning of one part of KP Dom, they found, or, that is, the Trial Chamber found that this position is sufficient to imply a significant contribution. There may seem to be a difference in standards between this standpoint taken by the Trial Chamber in the Krnojelac case and the judgements in Krstic and Tadic, the Krstic and Tadic trials. Although no judgement has yet been handed down by this Tribunal to the effect, or any standpoint taken, to the effect that the physical presence of a person in a place and at a time when the crimes falling under the jurisprudence of this Tribunal took place can be used to prove the culpability of that person. Additional evidence is needed, in addition to his physical presence at that place and time. In the view of this Defence team and the other Defence teams, this objective responsibility does not exist. Something more is needed. What is this? There has to be influence or authority, something that can be pointed to specifically. This, however, does not mean that the Prosecution did not have to prove the mens rea of the accused in connection with the crimes alleged against him and the crimes he allegedly perpetrated. The Defence feels that the Prosecution had to prove mens rea in connection with the crimes the accused is charged with. The Defence asserts that it is not sufficient for this conclusion to be possible. It has to be the only possible reasonable conclusion. If, on the basis of the evidence and the witness statements, there is any doubt or any other possible conclusion, then the Trial Chamber cannot draw this conclusion. In a situation when we are determining the position of an accused in a joint criminal enterprise, the Defence believes we have to proceed from what the Trial Chamber established in this case, namely, that these are people of very low rank. We're not talking about people who have any command responsibility or any command position. They are free. That is, Mr. Prcac is free of command responsibility envisaged by the Statute. So he can be responsible only individually. By making a significant contribution or by having enabled, unhindered or better functioning of the camp at the time. The Trial Chamber in this case derived this position from the Dachau case, where it says if the membership of an accused who is low-ranking and who was implied to be a member of a joint criminal enterprise, with guilt already presumed, could be exonerated if his contribution was insignificant, or less than significant, if his stay at the camp was short, and so on and so forth. In this case, the Trial Chamber accepted this position, and it says - that's paragraph 309 of the judgement - the mere presence of the accused at the camp does not mean that he is criminally responsible. His participation in that camp has to be significant, and that means that his acts or omissions make the enterprise more efficient and effective, and this is applicable on a case-by-case basis. This is a standard accepted by the Trial Chamber itself, and it is grounded in the position of this Tribunal as a whole. The Defence, therefore, had to prove that the accused did not have the position he was incriminated with and that he did not commit the acts he was charged with. The Prosecution did not have any reason, nor could they have envisaged, that some other function apart from the one they indicated increased his -- the accused's significance. So the position of the accused in this enterprise, aider and abettor, instigator, member, et cetera, becomes important. What has to be proven is whether Mr. Prcac, Dragoljub Prcac, did indeed make a significant contribution to the functioning of this camp. We claim that, no, and that he is not criminally responsible. If we look at the indictment, the Prosecution has claimed in this indictment - I will be brief here - that in the period from the 24th of May until the 30th of August, in his capacity of active policeman who replaced Miroslav Kvocka as deputy camp commander, was superior to everyone in the camp except the camp commander, and as deputy commander, had a possibility to change the conditions in the camp, to control the comings and goings of visitors, and to determine the regime. Following the indictment, our learned friend Keegan repeated all this and added some more. He claimed that in Omarska camp there was a clear hierarchy with Zeljko Meakic being the commander. He said that the position of Dragoljub Prcac, as deputy commander, gave him actual control over shift commanders and the visitors who came into the camp, such as Zigic, and that he was present during the commission of criminal acts, and that on several occasions he called out prisoners from previously prepared lists, lists that he was in charge of, that he was in control over all parts of the camp and that he performed the duties of the commander in the absence of Zeljko Meakic. Your Honours, as you know, the Defence made a comparative analysis of the charges levelled against the accused and between the findings of the Trial Chamber. Not a single count in the indictment has been proven by the Prosecution. Not proved by applying in dubio pro reo, for instance. We established who was in charge for the food, for the water. We established what the relations were in the camp, what the structure of the camp was, and it turned out that the claims of the Prosecution were untrue. On the other hand, in the response made by the Prosecution to the appeal made by this Defence team, the Prosecution attempt to swap theories, saying that the fact that he was not said to be the commander of the camp means that he is not culpable under Article 7(3) of the Statute. With all due respect, as far as I'm aware of international criminal law, I haven't found a single national legislation where the indictment is not obliged to specify exactly what somebody is charged with. If that something does not exist, then we don't need the indictment -- it is not needed at all. It is enough to say that somebody is part of a joint criminal enterprise, and then you can go on from that to prove any theory. What is curious is the following: The Appeals Chamber, after all, establishes certain standards at one point. I will deal with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. The Trial Chamber establishes certain standards. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] In paragraph 245 says that an indictment has to be very clear in specifying the charges, in order to enable the trying of the accused. This is the standard laid by the Trial Chamber but has not been observed in this case, in our view. So, as for the joint criminal enterprise itself and the participation of the accused Prcac in it, we need to emphasise that nowhere, in no way, was it established how his contribution was significant and what he has done for anyone to be able to claim that he participated in this joint criminal enterprise. The Defence stressed, and firmly believes, that the Trial Chamber made a series of grave errors. At this point, the Defence does not believe that the Trial Chamber weighed the evidence and testimonies and made findings that are disadvantageous to the Defence. The Defence claims that the Trial Chamber misquoted the transcripts, took things out of context, and misinterpreted the submissions of this Defence. These grave errors resulted in the erroneous conclusion made by the Trial Chamber that the accused Prcac was in charge of the camp and the commander, the administrative controller of the camp. We will deal with this later, however. No reasonable trier of fact, in our submission, could come to that conclusion. The finding of the Appeals Chamber that this Defence should not evaluate evidence -- but, however, we are not evaluating evidence. We are just submitting that certain evidence was not considered by the Trial Chamber. Similarly, the Trial Chamber established the principle in dubio pro reo. A lot of evidence was adduced, and the Trial Chamber decided that a great number of witnesses spoke about the role of Mr. Prcac in the Omarska camp. 37 spoke about the Omarska camp, the occurrences there, its structure; and 45 spoke about the role of Mr. Prcac. Out of the 37, some said that he was the commander. Some said -- in fact, four said that he was deputy commander. Some, in fact, one, said that he was the administrative assistant of the camp commander, and the rest didn't know at all what his role was. In keeping with the dubio pro reo principle, the Trial Chamber says that there is no evidence that he was the camp commander. But on the basis of the same evidence, the Trial Chamber goes on to conclude that he was the administrative assistant of the camp commander, instead of saying that there is no evidence of his role. The situation is similar with the standards applied by the very Trial Chamber, although these are the same principles against which we appealed, concerning, in particular, the evaluation of the credibility of witnesses and their testimony. It has been established for a long time in this Tribunal that witnesses cannot be expected to give precise testimony eight or nine years later after the event. It doesn't mean, however, that the witness can say whatever they want and the Trial Chamber can take out of that testimony what it needs. In practice, it boils down to one thing. Testimony which is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. inconsistent with previously given statements to the Prosecution is acceptable. Testimony which is inconsistent with other testimony is also acceptable, but only if they are minor inconsistencies. It is quite clear that a witness cannot remember everything very clearly. A witness speaks from memory. But an event can be described more or less precisely; but it cannot be completely different and fall out of the context created by the bulk of all the other testimony. Before this Trial Chamber, this Defence team has had a lot of problems. First of all, we did not receive any material which is being disclosed nowadays under Rule 68. And we were prejudiced because we didn't have one important fact that was proven in the Tadic case, but to the great regret of this Defence team, it was established wrongly. We could have been able to use this material, but we didn't. We were unable to produce this material before certain witness who testified here about certain circumstances. It happened many times during the trial that witnesses were replaced. It was the case with eight or nine witnesses. The credibility of witnesses was always -- was very often in question. The imperative should have been to establish the truth despite the limitations of time. It is the view of this Defence that we cannot accept the testimony of a witness which is disparate with the testimony of all the other witnesses. It happened in the Tadic case - and it is relevant for our case - that a witness testified who was later found not to have been the victim of rape at all. If such a witness was able to be called, that is completely wrong. Such things happened in our trial as well. As far as the Omarska camp is concerned, certain testimonies were drawn out of context, both regarding witness testimony and the submissions written by this Defence team. As I said, the third standard applied by the Trial Chamber was that the indictment should provide a recognisable framework and provide guidelines to the Defence as to what the accused is charged with and how he should be defended, against what. The Defence made clear in its appeal that the claim that the accused was administrative assistant to the camp commander is a grave violation of this standard. This Defence has never heard in this courtroom that anybody charged their client with being the administrative assistant to the camp commander. What is important to us at this moment is that the Trial Chamber was trying to establish a certain hierarchy and structure of the camp. And it established beyond any reasonable doubt - a point on which we agree - there was an investigative service, there was a special platoon of guards who were serving these investigators, then that there was an intervention squad from Banja Luka in one part of the camp. There was also a technical service that took care of the maintenance of facilities of the camp, that there was an army as an external security system, that there was a Territorial Defence that was in charge of preparing, supplying, and delivering food, and also helped provide security, the physical security of the camp. In this section, the Trial Chamber establishes that these services existed, and Zeljko Meakic, as the commander or security, had no competency, de facto or de jure; was unable to punish or control investigators or any other component of this structure. Although this was not said decisively, this finding of the Trial Chamber means that Zeljko Meakic was a chief of security, not camp commander. The indictment charges Dragoljub Prcac with being deputy commander of the camp, deputy to Zeljko Meakic. Now, look at the situation we are in. Zeljko Meakic is not camp commander. He is chief of security, whereas Prcac suddenly becomes deputy camp commander. And nobody knows - not the Trial Chamber, not the Defence teams, not the Prosecution - who the camp commander actually was. And the Defence team wonders how am I able to appeal at all, and what am I able to do in a situation when I do not know the identity of the camp commander? The camp commander is some fictive person which we, by the way, established to be Simo Drljaca, because the Trial Chamber didn't bother with it at all. So Zeljko Meakic was charged with being the deputy camp commander, whose identity, the identity of the camp commander being unknown. From the viewpoint of the Defence, we believe it is a very important issue indeed. First, if we take into consideration that the Defence was never shown that Dragoljub Prcac was perhaps the administrative assistant to the camp commander, and if his role was always linked to Zeljko Meakic, the chief of security, and we do not know who the camp commander was, the Defence asked itself, and this is a question we put forward in our brief, would we have conducted the defence in the same way had we known all this? The Defence could say that Dragoljub Prcac was -- or rather, the Prosecution could have said that Dragoljub Prcac had an important position in the camp, and then the Defence could have considered all the possibilities. However, throughout the trial, the Prosecution claimed that he was the deputy camp commander. The Defence attempted to prove that he was not, that he had not been the deputy camp commander. We were trying to establish all the time not what he did not do, but what he actually did; what he was actually in charge of. The Defence was not satisfied with a narrow interpretation of dubio pro reo. It was not satisfied with proving that he was not the deputy camp commander. We were rather concerned with showing what he actually did in the camp, and we adduced this. But the Trial Chamber misinterpreted what we presented completely. Not only did it misinterpret it, it cut off a part of a sentence, thereby giving it a completely different meaning. In the situation where we do not know who the camp commander was, we cannot examine the role of Mr. Dragoljub Prcac. There is not a shred of evidence to show that he contacted anyone but Zeljko Meakic, who was the chief of security. No evidence was ever adduced to prove this. If we put forward the hypothesis, as the Prosecution would like to do in their response to our appeal, that we should have foreseen, because he was indicted of being a member of a joint criminal enterprise, that we should have foreseen this, this would mean that in fact we didn't need the indictment at all. All we would need was this general information that he was part of a joint criminal enterprise. I really don't know what the Defence would have looked like in that case and what defence could have been put forward. With all our limitations and with all our very limited resources, I don't think any Defence team could have had a chance of proving the innocence of anyone before this Tribunal. Because if he was not the deputy commander, he was the administrative assistant. If he wasn't the administrative assistant, he might have been the cook. If not the cook, then the scribe. If not, then he might just have had influence, because perhaps he was an elderly person or a good person, a person people respected because he had never -- he had never had any conflicts with anyone and was respected in the community, and that would have been sufficient to declare him a war criminal because he was influential. If we look at the situation in the Omarska camp at the time when these crimes took place, we shall see that apart from the organisation which, in the view of the Defence, has been described with great precision, it is fair to say that there was chaos in the camp. Anyone could enter the camp. Evidently, anyone could maltreat, abuse, or even murder whoever they wanted to. And evidently, the Defence is not trying to claim that perhaps there was a plan. Somebody had to create this plan; that somebody had to have authority. He had to be in a certain position and he had to have people willing to implement the plan. But criminal responsibility cannot be inferred from position alone. This trial involves low-ranking persons. The highest rank in the police, whoever answered to this Tribunal was the chief of the patrol sector. We did not get the chief of police or anyone in a senior position. Those who actually created the criminal enterprise have not been indicted, those who worked on its implementation, on murders, on torture, on worsening the living conditions of the detainees. The Defence gave up on those people. 13 other accused were to have been indicted before this Tribunal. These are persons mentioned in the documents. These are persons mentioned by name as having perpetrated crimes. These are persons who did not perpetrate only one crime, they are people who consistently and constantly mistreated the detainees. If we look at the actual state of affairs, the guards in the camp, of whom there were six or seven or eight, that's number -- there are 13 of those. We are talking of people of the same of rank. In a village near Prijedor, which existed in the former Yugoslavia, this village was known for its football, its soccer club, which once played an important game, and it was known from World War II because of an enemy offensive on the village of -- on the mountain of Kozara. In that little village there was a police station, mostly manned by people who had not been properly trained or schooled, had only done some training courses. And these people were expected to have an overview of the general situation in relation to the former Yugoslav legislation, if omission or failure to act could not be a violation of international criminal law. These people were expected to understand the context and avoid such a situation. They were not so well informed or educated, and they felt that by not acting - that is, by not hitting a detainee, or doing anything to injure any of the detainees, or harm them in any way - they felt that they were keeping their distance from the joint criminal enterprise by doing nothing except helping, sometimes bringing some food, some medicine, within the scope of their possibilities. Because we have to understand that the overall situation in Prijedor was bad. Prijedor gravitated towards Zagreb and Belgrade. Both those lines of communication had been cut off. There was no economy. These were poor people. Apart from their employment, they had to do additional work in order to survive. The Defence talked about the case of Mr. Prcac. This was an ordinary man who felt that he could show his disagreement by not doing anything. He didn't understand the situation. The Defence put forward evidence showing that he was forced to go to the Omarska camp. We would never have put this forward as a ground of appeal had the Trial Chamber only stated in its judgement that it did not give credence to the statements that Mr. Prcac made in his interview that he gave to the Prosecution. No. Instead, they said that Mr. Prcac did not mention the fact that he had been forced into coming to the Omarska camp when he gave his interview to the Office of the Prosecutor. The Defence would like to point out that Mr. Prcac was arrested on the 5th of March. He met the Prosecution for the first time on the 6th of March. The trial began on the 2nd of May. So a certain period of time elapsed, or rather, 45 days, between his arrest and the start of trial. Almost nothing had been disclosed. We did not have the complete material. We still had the redacted witness statements. So the Defence and the accused were not fully aware of the facts and of the fact basis, and we felt that it was important for him to give an interview. He gave an interview. As you know much better than I do, an interview is a situation in which the Prosecution puts questions and the accused answers. As we did not know all the facts in the fact basis, in the Factual Basis, on the first day of the interview, Mr. Prcac gave his own view of the events in Prijedor and the Omarska camp, and then for a further three or four days the Prosecution put questions. And we have mentioned the pages of the transcript, and so on and so forth. In that interview, Mr. Prcac said that Simo Drljaca had threatened him with a bullet in the forehead and that his house would be burnt down unless he went to Omarska. The Trial Chamber said that Mr. Prcac never said this. This is the grave error that the Defence is drawing attention to.
