Had the Chamber said Mr. Prcac did say this but we did not give credence to it, he was saying this only to evade criminal responsibility, then the Defence would have viewed this as a prerogative of the Trial Chamber and would not have used it in our appeal. However, the Chamber claimed that he had never said this. The conclusion that Mr. Prcac was administrative assistant to camp commander is only one of many such errors. The first error that the Defence draws attention to is the situation as to whether he arrived -- whether he was coerced into going to the camp, under duress. The second error of the Trial Chamber consists in Mesan Omer's witness testimony. Various witnesses testified before this Tribunal, trying to explain the role and contribution of Mr. Prcac, and one of these witnesses described a situation in which Mr. Prcac allegedly, independently, without consulting his superiors, decided -- or rather, made the decision on the transfer of detainees. This allegedly took place on the 6th of August, when the camp was disbanded. After the 6th of August, 174 detainees remained. They had beds and food, and they were under the supervision of the ICRC, while all the others were transferred to the military camp at Manjaca or the Trnopolje collection centre. This happened on the last day, and all the witnesses say that a large number of guards were calling out detainees' names. So there wasn't a single one who was especially tasked to do this. There were about 1.700 or 800 men whose names were called out. They were put on buses and taken away. Then a number of men appeared who were not on any list, claiming that -- they claimed that Mr. Prcac had done this in order to demonstrate that he made a significant contribution and could act on his own initiative. Mr. Mesic said that he said: Take these men there. And that therefore they were transferred to Manjaca. On the basis of this, the Trial Chamber concluded that Mr. Prcac acted independently during the transfer of detainees, single-handedly, without consulting his superiors. But Mr. Omer did not recognise Mr. Prcac. Our question is: How can we say that this actually was Mr. Prcac? Although no one could conclude beyond any reasonable doubt that that person, whoever it was, was responsible for the transfer of detainees. This could have been somebody entirely different. But this is something that was stressed by the Trial Chamber and that led to Mr. Prcac being declared the administrative assistant to the camp commander. The Trial Chamber - and this is something that the Defence finds especially important - is that they said that Prcac was the administrative assistant to the camp commander. Your Honours, the Defence never stated this. The Defence adduced numerous quotations on the basis of which the real state of affairs can be ascertained, and that is that throughout the proceedings, the Defence, from its pre-trial brief onwards, consistently claimed that Dragoljub Prcac had been brought to the Omarska camp to work on radio communications and that from time to time he performed other jobs. These jobs were sometimes finding a certain detainee, drawing up a list of detainees who had just been brought in, or something else that he was commanded to do by Zeljko Meakic. In the structure of the camp, as established by the Trial Chamber, there is no doubt that investigators could give orders, because it was established beyond doubt that, in terms of hierarchy, the investigators were superior to the security service. And this is the only correct statement, the only correct piece of information, and the Defence does not know how and why the Trial Chamber was able to conclude what it concluded. Throughout the proceedings, the Prosecution attempted to portray Mr. Prcac as someone who held a position and that this was reflected in the fact that he drew up lists of detainees. They drew this conclusion from the fact that all the witnesses who testified about Mr. Prcac said that he only occasionally walked about the compound and that he usually carried sheets of paper with him. Nobody ever said that he carried Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. lists, or if they did say so, this was pure speculation. Wishing to add weight to this, the Prosecution started saying that he was in fact responsible for the lists that were drawn up, lists of people to be liquidated. And, as we heard a moment ago, the Defence did not wish to hide at any point from anything by saying something didn't happen. We tried to find out exactly what lists were made, how, and what the people from those lists had ended like. We had one such witness who was responsible, in the first part of the existence of the camp, for the making of all those notorious lists. Asked who placed detainees into three categories - because the Prosecution insisted on these three categories, that is, combatants, abettors, and those to be released - categories on the basis of which triage was made. And most of these were non-Serbs. This witness said: It was me. I had to decide on a methodology to be used for triage, and that's how we did it. And this witness explained how it came about that Mr. Prcac read out a list of women who, fortunately, are all alive and were all transferred to Trnopolje camp. There is no evidence - except in one single case, but fortunately, there are other elements of proof to the same point - there is no evidence that anyone who was driven away or transferred from the camp called out by Mr. Prcac was never seen again. There is only one person, Eso Sadikovic, from Prijedor. He was called out by Prcac and he was exhumed later in a mass grave in Hrastova Glavica, together with 124 prisoners from Keraterm. There is enough evidence of that to prove that he was taken to Keraterm and met his death 90 days later. That's the only person who was called out by Mr. Prcac. And Mr. Prcac did mention him in his interview. The Defence, in fact, claims that everything mentioned by Mr. Prcac in his interview proved to be correct. So, this begs the question - and I don't want to take any more time of the Appeals Chamber, because you are familiar with our submissions - all these errors, misquotations and misinterpretations, were used in order to proclaim Mr. Prcac deputy commander of the camp, or administrative assistant to the camp commander, and thus increase his criminal responsibility. The Trial Chamber at no point defines his contribution. In one paragraph, it says that he obviously had some influence among the guards over whom he had no superiority, and the same goes for guards. He took care of the transfer of prisoners inside the camp, on the orders of Meakic's investigators, and that is his contribution. Because of all these situations that the Defence has mentioned now, the Defence stressed the evaluation of credibility of certain witnesses. We're not talking about minor irregularities. We're talking about huge differences in testimony, huge disparities. And the Trial Chamber, unfortunately, took out certain testimonies that have not been corroborated by any other testimony, out of the context to place Mr. Prcac in the position of administrative assistant. Without this qualification, Mr. Prcac would not have been convicted. That's what the Defence is trying to show. We are trying -- we were trying to show to the Trial Chamber that by analysing all the evidence, it can be established realistically, beyond any reasonable doubt, that his position was very low; below that of a regular guard. According to what the Trial Chamber established, certain people with certain positions walked around the camp. Some people gave them special meaning. At one point, it was said: Witness A said this to him: And other witness said yes, they were there, talking and they left. And Witness A says: Well, no, actually, I didn't hear that they were giving an order, as she claimed previously. There were many such cases. Without proving that position, his contribution cannot be proven. If we now look at the Dachau judgement, the standard is long-term contribution. 22 days may be long term, even if you are not there all the time. But Mr. Prcac was in the camp only 11 times, during 11 shifts. I don't know if even Karadzic or Mladic, had they been in the camp at all, would be able to establish order in the camp. In addition, as soon as he arrived at the camp, he expressed his dissatisfaction. He asked why a dead man was lying on the ground; why there was no chlorine; why there was no food. Simo Drljaca answered -- somebody answered to him that Simo Drljaca ordered it this way. Prcac brought food to the camp. Another witness was saying that she was regularly called out at night, insinuating that she was maybe raped. And this woman said: Mr. Prcac probably saved my life. In the context of all these situations and incidents, we have to bear in mind this witness who was maybe raped, said that she went to talk to Mr. Prcac because he could give her comfort, and she said that my family is alive because of Mr. Prcac, because he took care of them, he comforted them. Many evidence was adduced here to prove that non-Serbs had to sign away their property to Republika Srpska before they were able to leave Prijedor. It was a statement, a legal statement. In that situation, Mr. Prcac makes a document of legacy with another person. And when she came back, her weekend cottage was already destroyed. The apartment was no longer available because it was the property of the municipality, and that's the whole story. The Omarska camp existed. The conditions were inhumane. They were atrocious. And that's what we should be dealing with: Who is responsible for that, rather than trying to replace them by these low-ranking people, trying to reason that they could somehow be connected with the real perpetrators. In that context, how is it impossible not to incriminate people who constantly committed crimes, who did have discriminatory intent? Nothing was shown before the Trial Chamber, nor was it written in the judgement, to the effect that Mr. Prcac had discriminatory intent in his actions. So much about discriminatory intent. The Defence will not deal with it any more. So all that was claimed or charged by the Prosecution has not been proven. The question arises: Is the Trial Chamber entitled to go beyond the scope of the indictment and decide on facts that are not mentioned there, to decide that an accused is guilty of other things, simply by being a member of the joint criminal enterprise? If that were so, that would mean that we don't need indictments at all. It would be enough to say that such-and-such a person was there, and by that mere fact was guilty. After the end of the Prosecution case, the Defence made a motion under Rule 98 bis for acquittal, and even then we claimed that there is not enough evidence to find Mr. Prcac guilty of the charges beyond any reasonable doubt. We signaled in that submission that there is not enough evidence. And the Prosecution could have amended the indictment at that stage. Another option open to them was to write a longer, more detailed indictment that would lead our Defence to investigate into other possibilities concerning the role of Dragoljub Prcac in the camp. No. Throughout their case, the Prosecution claimed that he was deputy camp commander, which determined his role and his significant contribution. In conclusion, we should say that the Prosecution didn't appeal at all. We shouldn't lose sight of those pictures from Keraterm, from Trnopolje, rather, made by Penny Marshall in her programme, and that immediately after the Vukovar events, this Tribunal was established. Justifiably or not, truthfully or not, the Omarska camp was present and highlighted everywhere as one of the greatest atrocities anywhere, certainly in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. And when you bring here persons accused of contributing to the Omarska camp, you don't appeal. You claim that you have the structure of the camp firmly established and that those are the people. When Mr. Prcac gets five years, he is not expected to appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, are you proposing to leave a few minutes for questions by the Judges? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, certainly, of course. I will be done very shortly. So, in conclusion, Your Honour, I would like to stress that this Tribunal was not established to settle accounts with people who were physically present in an area. It has been said many times what the level of this Tribunal is. It is the highest legal, judicial body in this part of the world. We established that my client had the status of a regular guard, he had no command responsibility. The Trial Chamber went beyond the context and that it was not regular for somebody to be convicted of a charge absent from the indictment. And it is not the task of the Trial Chamber to save the indictment and do the job of the Prosecution. It would not be awful for a Serb to be acquitted, in our submission, especially if nothing in the indictment has been proven. So much, Your Honour, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'm much obliged to you, Mr. Simic. Let me see if my colleagues on the Bench wish to clarify anything in your statements. Judge Guney wants to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Simic, in the course of your submission, you have attempted to highlight the influence and the authority that your client had at the camp. You insisted on the fact that he was not camp commander. Is that true? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] We said that he was not only not camp commander. We said throughout the trial that he was not deputy camp commander, as alleged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Simic. Please proceed. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Well, if the interpretation is correct, and if I understood the question correctly, we claimed that he was not deputy camp commander, as written in the indictment, and that we have proven. That was established by the judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have carefully listened to your submission, in which you emphasised the fact that your client was replacing Kvocka between 24th of May until the 30th of August. Is that true? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry, but it is not true. We were saying exactly the reverse. Mr. Prcac did not replace Miroslav Kvocka, and even the Trial Chamber established that. And therefore, will you bear with me for a minute. If he had been a deputy, then he would have been deputy of the chief of security, as the Trial Chamber found Mr. Kvocka to have been. But they say there is no evidence of that and there is no evidence of him being the deputy commander or the deputy chief of security, and that's why they proclaimed him administrative assistant instead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the light of what you said, would you kindly give me your view: Who, according to you, was the commander of the Omarska camp? Second: Tell me kindly, what was the exact position, the exact function of your client for the duration of his stay in the camp? What duties did he discharge as long as he was there? I would like clarification on these two points, if possible. Thank you. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of the Defence, it was Simo Drljaca who was the camp commander, or rather, the Crisis Staff. According to the witness statements, mainly Defence witnesses, but also some Prosecution witnesses, Simo Drljaca certainly had a major influence. The investigators, who were the most important service, reported to him daily. No one could be arrested without his order or approval, nor could anyone be released without his order or approval. Furthermore, he was the person who decided on everything. He visited the camps on more than one occasion. All the services, according to testimony from other cases, because I've read all the transcripts, reported to him and to the Crisis Staff. We asserted all the time that it was Simo Drljaca who was the camp commander. No evidence was ever adduced, nor did anyone speculate, that Mr. Dragoljub Prcac was in any kind of contact or relationship with Simo Drljaca. It was Simo Drljaca who was the camp commander. There were four or five services acting independently, but all reporting to Simo Drljaca. They were acting independently of each other. They all had their positions and their duties. And you also asked me about the position of the accused Prcac. I have to say that Prcac came to the camp just before the camp was disbanded. Before that he was a forensic technician in the Omarska area. On the 15th of July, or around the 15th of July, he was brought with a clear task, to maintain the radio connection, because, according to witness testimonies, the radio connection was maintained by ordinary guards who did not always know how to cope with the technology, so it was necessary to bring in somebody who was familiar with radio technology and who could maintain the connection with the police department, because there was no direct telephone line. There was one that the investigators had, but it was in a locked room. And in that period, in which there were 11 shifts, he was occasionally present when detainees were brought in, on orders from Meakic or the investigators, and as there were no records or lists, as the Prosecution wanted to show, the detainees wandered around, and if an investigator wanted to question someone, he had to send somebody to find this detainee and bring him to him. These were the kinds of jobs that he was asked to do, to locate a certain detainee, to be present when detainees were brought in. Investigators -- or the witnesses didn't testify to seeing him a lot because he was next to the radio equipment. He had no talent, no special knowledge. He did jobs that everybody did. The Defence brought mostly witnesses who had been at the camp, and these were all people who did exactly the same jobs as he did. A guard sometimes received detainees. Prcac didn't sit there around the clock. He had his 12-hour shift, and he was always there when Meakic was there. So if we look at the Celebici case, the deputy commander cannot be held responsible if the commander is present. But that was not the case, actually. He did only the kinds of jobs that everybody did. There was nothing to set him apart specially in what he did. He was not specifically in charge of any segment of the work there. He did carry sheets of paper around, so somebody thought that he was an administrator of some sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Guney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Counsel. The principal function of your client was technical. He was in charge of radio communications. But nevertheless, he did keep lists of detainees and he fulfilled certain tasks of that kind. Is that task compatible with the technical duty, with a technical position, and to what degree? I would like to hear your opinion. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with all due respect, I think his fundamental task could not be reduced to that of a technician. This was only a part of his duties. This was something that was done in all police stations or police departments in the former Yugoslavia where there was an institution of a duty officer or someone, and these were rotated. They switched around. There was no single person tasked with carrying out this duty. So that everybody did various jobs up there. The guards mostly stood there. It was very warm. And Zeljko Meakic, as the chief of security, probably wanted to make it easier for them so that they wouldn't have to stand around all the time. So his main task was not the technical equipment but maintaining the connection, because the Omarska police department at that moment covered the Omarska camp in providing security, and also they had to secure the village of Omarska and Petrov Gaj, Kevljani, Maricke and the other hamlets. So that there had to be a communications link between the police department and the camp, if Zeljko Meakic had to be called in or the medical corps had to be called in. This was a technical communications line that had to be maintained by all the guards. And as Your Honour has observed, the investigators who carried Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. out the triage, who decided who was to be put in what category and what their fate was to be, they would be looking for a certain detainee to question him. So they could ask either Prcac or a guard, or anybody else, to find him. When new detainees were brought in, although in that period, they were not brought in on a large scale but only individually, and then again the investigators, or Simo Drljaca, as we have shown in our evidence, would give names of people to be arrested, and when they arrived, their details were taken down and then this was taken to the investigators, who decide whether to call him in for questioning or not. He did nothing unique, nothing specific, nothing that everybody else didn't do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I turn to my colleagues on my left. Judge Mumba has question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Simic, following your submissions on the role of Mr. Prcac, I note that in sum - correct me if I'm wrong - what you're saying is that he had a minor role to play in the running of the camp, albeit his services were necessary for the running of the camp at the material time. Is it your submission, then, that considering the minor role that the appellant was playing at the camp, what he did, did not amount to serious violations? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I say, "Minor role," what we were trying to say is that he did nothing different from what all the other guards did, the guards who have not been indicted. So his actions and omissions, in our view, do not constitute serious violations of humanitarian law. Otherwise, they would all have had to be indicted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Weinberg de Roca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have only one short question. Mr. Simic, you, a few minutes ago, mentioned that the Trial Chamber relied on the credibility of one witness whose testimony was very different from all the others that testified on one event. Could you specify to what you're referring to? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is Witness Nusret Sivac, and he has been specially dealt with in the final brief of the Defence. We attempted to prove that he told eight serious untruths before the Trial Chamber. Nusret Sivac said that he was moved from Mujo's room to the pista, the concrete, because water was available there, but he was the only one who claimed that Dragoljub Prcac was in charge of all administrative duties in the Omarska camp. No other witness said anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just one little question, Mr. Simic. If I may say so, I found your submissions helpful. Would you help me to understand something. I want you to focus on that part of your submissions in which you said something to the effect that your client really went to Omarska camp under something in the nature of duress, and that he had been threatened by Drljaca with a bullet in his head if he didn't go. So I want you to focus on that. Now, it is my impression that your case is that the Trial Chamber misquoted some of the evidence on that point. I am entirely with you on this distinction. You can have a case in which the court misquotes the evidence, and you can have a case in which the court quotes the evidence correctly but, for good and sufficient reasons, it does not accept the evidence. Now, I have looked at paragraph 427 of the judgement of the Trial Chamber on this point, as to the circumstances in which your client went to Omarska and whether he had been threatened by Drljaca. Is there anything in that paragraph which answers to my impression that your case is that the Trial Chamber misquoted the evidence on the point? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me just briefly look at the judgement, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Paragraph 427. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this paragraph is correct. There is a paragraph in which something else is stated, that the Trial Chamber was not convinced of this because Prcac never mentioned any threats when he was interviewed by the Prosecution. This is in another paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: But in this same paragraph, does not the Trial Chamber say the same thing in the penultimate section -- sentence, it says: The Trial Chamber notes, however, that Prcac never mentioned any threats when he was interviewed by the Prosecution. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Correct. Correct. Yes. So in this paragraph too, they say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then, we will adjourn for the moment and return one hour and 30 minutes later on, that is, at 2.45. Yes. 2.45. Would that be agreeable, Mr. Fila? 2.45, then. We will return at 2.45. Thank you, for the moment. The Court is now adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.17 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Members of the bar, this sitting is resumed. We will now hear learned counsel Mr. Fila -- oh, I'm sorry. I didn't notice you. Go ahead, Mr. Simic. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'll be very brief, but I feel that there might have been a misunderstanding in response to your question. So may I be allowed to give an additional explanation with respect to the quotation from the judgement itself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do forgive me. I've lost the place. What place was I referring to? What paragraph? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Paragraph 427, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] May I have your permission to explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, your question was, I think, whether this paragraph reflects the assertions made by the Defence, that is to say, that the Trial Chamber assumed the position that, as Mr. Prcac never mentioned in an interview to the Prosecution that he came under threat and coercion, whether this paragraph expresses that position. In the last two sentences, it says: "The Trial Chamber notes, however, that Prcac never mentioned any threats when he was interviewed by the Prosecution." We claim in our appellant brief that he did, and I think this is something that the Defence has already brought out. And then the sentence reads, "The Trial Chamber is not convinced that these threats took place and does not accept his assertion that he worked at the camp under duress." So we claim that Prcac did mention threats and coercion under which he came to be in the camp, whereas the Trial Chamber claims that he did not mention it during an interview by the Prosecution. So what we are saying, once again, that he was under threat and it was not volitional on his part, et cetera, et cetera. That's what I wanted to bring up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic. You have clarified a point of importance to me. Thank you very much. Then we will hear you, Mr. Fila, for Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, Your Honours. This is a trial that has lasted for six years. It is a little unusual, if we compare it to all the others that I have taken part in, because three sets of Prosecutors have replaced each other, with three approaches to this case and these proceedings. And the proceedings have ended a little strangely as well, unusually. There is no appeal from the Prosecution with respect to the sentence itself, the number of years, but nothing with which we started out with is to be found in the judgement. I was a little surprised because I never understood one point. If I assert something and the Court does not find that that is so, that I could pass over that and then accept what the Court says and not what I was presenting as the case. If you look at the transcript, I dealt with the Statute quite a bit, the Statute of this august Tribunal. At the beginning of this very lengthy trial, I commented and objected to the differences in this Statute and the statute of the court in Rwanda, and you will remember that it was Common Article 9 of the Geneva Conventions. And the Trial Chamber ruled that I was not right. That was not a happy event for me, but what can I do? I have to move on and accept it. The second point that I dealt with was Article 2 of the Statute of this Tribunal and its definition of what serious violations of the Geneva Conventions means. I would be very happy if, after eight years spent in this Tribunal, we could clear that matter up, or rather, you could clear that matter up for us once and for all. Now, why am I asking this? I am asking not only because this is something which concerns me in the sexual attacks with respect to Mr. Radic, who is my client. If something is a serious violation, then there is something that is not a serious violation, although the violation of any human right is a serious matter. But there must be some differentiation in quality between what is serious, serious violation and just a violation. Now, bearing in mind your very long experience, especially you, Mr. President, in the previous court, I'm sure you will come up with that solution and give it to us. Now, the question arises whether this is in my interests as a lawyer per se or as my lawyer in this case. You will see that when it comes to sexual assault - if I can put it that way, to put it under this heading of sexual assault - there are four individuals who said that Mladjo Radic performed some sort of improper acts towards them. Now, we questioned that he ever did anything of that kind. And I want to say that at the outset, not to have to enter into polemics later on, either with the judgement or the Prosecution's response, et cetera, et cetera. The position of Mr. Radic is that none of that is true, so that there was no acquiescence or anything like that. Let's forget that, and it's not essential in this case either. Now, whether these acts, or rather, what is the question that I wish to put here and now? If we were to exempt rape, leave rape out, would the other four acts represent serious violations of the Geneva Conventions, as is stated, without the act of rape itself? Probably not. However, the second question that comes to mind in this regard is that if once we establish that a camp such as Omarska, it has been established without doubt that there were serious violations of human rights - not only of the Geneva Conventions, but human rights as well. So once you have generally established that there were serious violations, then each and every act of violation which is not a serious violation can become a serious violation because it comes within this general heading of serious violations. So that is the problem that has been bugging me for a number of years now. And one of the judges will remember the Dokmanovic trial where the charges were that he watched for three and a half minutes while people were beaten at Ovcara and we had a lengthy discussion as to what this meant. He had died since and we never learnt about it. Had he remained with us, and it was Judge Mumba, she would probably have brought in a judgement and then I wouldn't have to ask this question. But that is the important question and point, as far as I'm concerned. Now, the third question that I should like to raise once again has to do with the Statute. It is Article 7(4), in fact, of the Statute. We are discussing an indictment here under 7(1) and 7(3) and we have established that there was no 7(1) but that there was Article 7(1) accountability and 7(3), and the Trial Chamber established that, as well as the fact that the Crisis Staff was formed in Omarska camp, and this was established on several occasions, and that Drljaca was a sort of commander. But one thing is incontestable, that the police station department of Omarska quite certainly, not only beyond reasonable doubt, but beyond any doubt at all, has anything to do with the organisation of that camp -- at all, in any way. So we have as something that is incontestable that an order is arriving and that the police station department - and I emphasise the word department because there is nobody else there but the chief, who is Medic [phoen]. All the others were ordinary policemen. So what we have is this: We have the police station department in Omarska which pursuant to an order one morning has to provide security for that camp, the Omarska camp. Now, if we look at Article 7(4) carefully of this Statute, which is in fact the result of the Nuremberg trials that orders do not justify the execution by a subordinate of those orders but can be a mitigating circumstance, I am worried that nobody has dealt with that question, and I think that it is a very important question, especially when we come to the lower-level individuals, down the chain of command. Of course, we can't talk about this at the Milosevic trial, for example, or Sainovic, who is my client, because that is a very high level, top level. But we're now talking about the lowest level, right down the chain of command. And this is referred to in Article 7(4), and so this is worthy of discussion, this matter, I believe. I don't like to try anybody's patience, and so I will end there as far as the Statute is concerned. Now, as far as the appellant's brief is concerned itself, I would like to say that it has been written in a fair amount of detail. I'm sure you have read it. That is normal. And so has the Prosecution because I have read their response, and I have replied to the Prosecution's response. I have an apology to make. At one point it says that the camp was in existence for two months. I apologise. That was a mistake. It was in existence for three months. That is the only typographical error that exists in the appellant's brief. But now it is not my intention to repeat what I say in the brief. I know that you are people who understand what has been written down and don't have to be told things three times. But I would nonetheless like briefly to go through the brief and indicate that some of these five reasons, the five grounds for appeal that I have set out are to be expounded. In the first grounds for appeal, the reasons we set out is the right to the accused to a fair trial. Because I consider that the judgement did not reflect that. And I set that out in three parts myself. As a form of criminal liability, the confidential schedules and facts as to conduct. I'm going to say just one or two sentences about each of these three points, because I consider, particularly because I belong to continental law and our source is Roman law, as you know full well. The Yugoslav Criminal Code was shaped according to the German Criminal Code and it is like that today and dates back to the kingdom of Yugoslavia, to the dark periods of Communism and it's true to the present day. But we always link up the identity of the indictment and the judgement, if I could put it that way, and that is a holy Bible for us. We abide by it. So when we deliberate in this way, our deliberations sometimes are like a horse with blinkers on when he is pulling a cart. That is how we view an indictment, like a horse with blinkers on. With all due respect to Your Honours, I have not seen here anything like the identity of the indictment and the judgement and the rapport between the two. Let me digress. The difference between the public at large and we lawyers is that we are well versed in the law and not in the facts. Anybody can see the facts. You go to the cinema, you see some facts presented to you. If we do not adhere to form, if we do not respect form and structure our results will be catastrophic and it is the form and structure which is important and it means that each Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. individual must know what he is being accused of. Not in any of the amended indictments is there criminal liability as a joint criminal enterprise. No liability for that. It just does not exist. In the introduction it says Keegan said so-and-so. But, as I say, three Prosecution teams replaced each other during the Prcac trial alone. So outside the Statute, leaving aside the statutory questions, which I'm sure you'll solve in the proper manner, let me clarify. Is the indictment important or is it just a general act? And having said that, let me remind you that in the introductory address of the late Dokmanovic, Mr. Niemann, who I otherwise respect, says that the indictment is not there to deal with matters of that kind, but that it should say that the person that I am charging has committed some criminal act and it is up to the Court to determine which. Because if the Prosecutor defines the criminal acts, he runs the risk of going wrong, making mistakes and then having the accused go free. And I think that was what one of your members said at one time. However, pursuant to Rule 50, with the -- or rather, the Prosecution violated Rule 50 by amending the indictment by putting forward the facts and evidence during the trial itself. So we're dealing with Rule 50 and the amendment of the indictment and how this was done by the Prosecutor. And as far as that is concerned, let me end with one sentence, quoted from your own judgement, in which you say the following: The Trial Chamber rather states the basic purpose of an indictment is to offer the accused a description of the acts committed, with sufficient detail for him to be able to prepare his defence and that therefore it must articulate the specific acts that the accused is alleged to have committed. So that is your judgement in the Kupreskic case. And let me follow on in that same vein. In Krnojelac, it says concrete characteristics and precision is what is required of the indictment. And in my own appellant's brief this is what I say myself, because you have legal practice taken from many other case and proceedings. Now, I'd like to say a few words about confidential schedules. And by a decision of the Trial Chamber, and we are appealing on that, the dilemma has been cleared up as to what confidential schedules actually mean, and the Trial Chamber has rendered the decision that it is part and parcel of the indictment. However, the object of our appeals brief is to concretise the indictment and not to mask over its individual parts and to give additional details to the accused of the crimes he is alleged to have committed and for which he has been charged. Because these are the requests, I'm coming back to the Statute now, Articles 18 and 21. But for this Trial Chamber, the previous Trial Chamber whose decision we are appealing, does not deal with that. It does not say anything about the facts that are contained in the schedule, in the confidential schedules and in that way thereby making the rights of the accused. Because as I said, the Trial Chamber is violating the spirit of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence by declaring the accused guilty in relation to certain counts but failing to mention the incidents which are contained in the relevant counts. Then we again come to evidence about the consistency of behaviour. This is something that continental law does not recognise but the Anglo-Saxon law does, and I respect that. What are we doing? We have Witness AT. The trial says: The alleged rape of AT was not mentioned in the amended indictment because of fairness to the accused, you cannot introduce charges against him in the middle of a trial without prior notice. For us, this was like a stone dropping from the sky. I would like you to look at the indictment under which Radic was arrested. He was charged with the rape of one single person, Witness A, of which he was acquitted here. To this very day, there is footage on television, Dutch, Bosnian, all televisions, that this same witness in another case, her testimony was accepted and she is saying that she was raped. Even Judge Riad participates in this TV footage. This is something that the Trial Chamber did not believe and this should be a mitigating circumstances. And the Prosecution did not object to that, even though they insisted in the Tadic case and insisted on that in this case here. And we have case closed. The witness is not held criminally liable, and the Bosniak intelligence service then finds a new witness. And now we will come to the witnesses later. But here again I'm talking about the legal aspects. Facts is something that we should not discuss with you. Let's discuss legal issues now, and above that we are -- in that matter we have above just lay people in this legal sense. We are talking about Rule 93(B) now. What does it say? It says that we should be informed about what is going to happen, that the client should be informed about what is going to happen. Do you know why this was not done? Because the Prosecution did not even know what they were going to use Witness AT for and that is why they didn't do that and simply 93(B) was not respected. These are violations of the Rules of Procedure, which would have an effect under Article 25 of the Statute to these proceedings. I'm not saying that the Trial Chamber was biased towards the Prosecution. Why would it be so? I have a very esteemed opinion about each single member of the Trial Chamber and their contribution to the case is priceless. But, unfortunately, are we making something here that we have unfortunately in our law, let us save the indictment at any cost? So that as far as consistency, consistent pattern of conduct is concerned, this rule is being violated. And once you violate the form, then the decision cannot be proper. Which means that I am claiming that in accordance with Rule 93, what was violated is violated the right of the accused to a fair trial, as well as the Rules of Procedure. And therefore, truth was violated as well. Our next ground for appeal, I'm going to deal with this in a summary fashion. In my second pattern, I talked about the form of criminal responsibility, and I'm speaking about this in two parts, joint criminal enterprise - it's difficult to translate into Serbian - and the role of the accused in this joint criminal enterprise. Now again we're talking about the question of theory, according to the position of the Defence. I'm not claiming that we are right, but this is my opinion, this is our take. The Trial Chamber must prove or show evidence that would demonstrate that the accused was part of that joint criminal enterprise that the accused Mladjo Radic was a part of that, and as a co-perpetrator at that. However, I did not find anything like that in the judgement. None of us normal, sensible people could say that Omarska is something that everyone has to be ashamed of. Of course, this is -- we're not denying that, and this is the opinion of this Court as well. We're talking about Omarska, Vukovar, and other places. But do you know what the most terrible injustice is? You are qualified to be just. We're talking about a completely different type of people who were involved in those things. What I would like to say, I would give you my reasons why these things cannot apply to the accused. You know very well from written information that Omarska was founded and established by an order of Simo Drljaca. Is it difficult, then, to understand what a small police department, a small village police department, is? Mladjo Radic had the lowest possible police rank. There was nobody below him. He was just a plain patrolman. They called him Krkan. He liked to eat. That was his nickname. And he lives in a village where probably the biggest problem is if somebody steals a chicken or gets drunk in a cafe. I'm not separating him in the sense that I wanted to imply that everybody else is bad. But what I'm saying is that a war has broken out. Nobody wanted this war. Some of them were even married to these Bosniaks. This war broke out that nobody wanted, and a person called Simo Drljaca, who was a nothing before that, forms some kind of camp, and they are ordered to go there. Would you please look at the interview of Mladjo Radic, and you will see typical things: I came to the bus station and they told me today you are going to Omarska. So can we not establish the physical and psychological state of that man, what his state of mind is, what is his position, what is he doing at all? And then suddenly we pushed him into something in order to justify some kind of indictment. Well, we probably do have people who are responsible for something like that. We have Zeljko Meakic, who was the head of security, and this was finally established. When he was arrested, he was the commander of the camp. When they were arrested he was the commander of the camp. He was even charged with genocide, which was later dropped, but I just wanted to remind you of that. But not to dwell on this too much. We have all of these things that were said, bad water -- the water is still bad. I've even brought samples. The water that they drank in 1992, they're still drinking today. It's a difficult question that there were insufficient quantities and that the living situation was different, but the actual quality of the water is the same now as it was then. I stated at the beginning and I stated that consistently and the Trial Chamber accepted that there was an uncontrolled willfulness prevalent in the camp. And this is clear. And then we must understand that if there was wilfulness, if anybody could beat or kill whomever they wanted, how is it possible for a police officer of the lowest rank to participate in something like that? I'm stating this on purpose. I absolutely accept the position of the Appeals Chamber about the three categories required for a joint criminal enterprise. There is no dispute about that. That is how it is. It is a decision that you made, and in the same way I'm asking you to decide on these other issues. But where is Mladjo Radic in all of this? We are discussing all these matters. They don't even go for aiding and abetting, as far as Mladjo Radic is concerned, but they go directly to him being a co-perpetrator. Where is the explanation for that? There is no explanation. The first conditions need to be met that he's a co-perpetrator, that is, direct intent. What kind of a direct intent can we talk about? He's given an order and then he's told you'll be there for three or four days. And this is what the Trial Chamber accepted. When they accepted, they went there for two or three days, or three or four days, but it actually ended up lasting for three or four months. So the first one is direct intent. For the second case --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters ask the counsel to read that back again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what is his position? There is this film that they're constantly showing against him where you can see him with a machine-gun across his chest. It just indicates that he is a plain police officer, and this is what we are claiming from the beginning. Which other leaders did you see with a picture of him taken at a guard post with a weapon? You know that guards usually are at guard posts. We didn't see Simo Drljaca have a picture of himself taken in this way. And now he says that an aider, an abettor can be somebody and they can become a co-perpetrator if this act lasts for a longer period of time or if he personally participants in it. If we leave aside the rape, with all due with respect to the Prosecutor who does not wish to have anything left aside, but I still would like to leave certain things aside in my explanation of the appeal grounds. So if we leave that aside, what is it that stays? And we will discuss this later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, you mentioned a second case, and at that point the interpreter asked you to read that back again. What did you have to read back? You don't know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Okay. No problem. [Interpretation] Well, it doesn't matter. We will read something else. Never mind. And now the Defence would finally like to say that the Trial Chamber, in spite of these three conditions, did not say what is the participation of the accused Radic in all of that? What part did he play in all of this? In the Krnojelac case, the second Trial Chamber, Trial Chamber II, said that the responsibility for common purpose is required evidence that the accused is implicated to a considerable degree in the implementation of such acts. Perhaps he is, and perhaps he's not, but that is not said explicitly. And if it is, if he did, then it should be stated. So this is the position that I quoted. There's no need for me to go into it again. So allow me to conclude. The Trial Chamber, deciding on the guilt of the accused Radic for persecution, failed to determine the pre-conditions as they were given in the previous paragraph. They do not determine the existence of agreement, shared intent with those committing the crime, together with those who are committed that [as interpreted]. And who did the persecutions? The Crisis Staffs, Simo Drljaca, and these were just the people who were implementing it, in the same way as cooks were implementing it. I cannot determine the difference. Radic's wife was a cook in that camp; she was baking bread and making food and taking it up there. Had she not taken food up there, they would probably have left their guard posts and these others would then have escaped. But we cannot go that far. I know the Munchausen case. My father was there for two years. I know what this looks like, and I know that it is terrible. But there has to be a limit somewhere. We must place a boundary somewhere. And that is, with all due respect, your task specifically for us to -- to tell us what the boundaries are. From here to here, we have grave violations of the Geneva Conventions, and from here to here it is not. We have local courts, thank God, and these things then can be tried over there. I believe that the Trial Chamber erred when they held that the participation of Radic was assessed as considerable. First of all, he had to have been a part of that in the military sense, as a co-perpetrator, because that is what he was charged with and then his acts also need to be significant. And again, I do not see that significance. I reiterate that for as long as I'm talking about this, I ask you to leave aside the rape. So in a part of my submissions, I'm making him equal to Kos. I did not manage to see it. It is nowhere explained in the substantial judgement what is the accused Radic's substantial contribution in these acts, including ethnic cleansing, killing, but also persecutions, that for sure. And then I must conclude that the Trial Chamber, the standards that it set applied in the wrong way, and the standard was to determine or establish considerable participation in the joint criminal enterprise. And I did not see that there in the judgement. The third ground of appeal are persecutions. I did say a lot about that already, and there's no need to say much more because we will all be dealing with that issue. I allow that you've already heard that from one Simic. You will hear about it from the other Simic. I share their opinion and therefore I can skip the next 50 pages of my appeal. The fourth grounds, and I mention that on page 31, is that the factual basis was wrongfully established for grounds number 4, that his participation in the acts in Omarska were greater than they were and that also his role in connection to what the other guards perpetrated was also wrongfully perpetrated. It was established that inmates were killed and ill-treated by anybody, whoever wanted to do so, without any encouragement from anybody else. People did not listen to his orders, Radic's orders. Conditions in the camps and how it all was, the Trial Chamber also itself found that this had nothing to do with Radic, and so I don't Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. know why it would be significant what -- what the significance of his acts would be within the whole framework of the camp if these things are not considered to be important. So my position is that the Trial Chamber wrongfully concluded about the role of Mladjo Radic in the Omarska camp, as I have already said several times. And now I would like to move to the most important point of my appeal. As you can see, I'm trying to spare you from too many details. With the liability under 7(3) of the accused, we contested this because we said that it wasn't clear whether he had effective control over the guards. And in dubio pro reo, he was freed of that charge. However, if he did not have that, what separated him from the other guards? What set him apart from the other guards? Because when you answer one question, you must answer the next one. If the Trial Chamber found that he did not have any control, then how was he different from the others? And this brings me to my starting point, that the witnesses, numerous witnesses asserted that Mladjo Radic was a guard like everybody else, and the Prosecution found that the others should be tried, if they are brought to trial, in their own country and not be brought to the Tribunal here. I feel the need to say this now, and it refers to Mr. Radic's assistance to certain detainees. There's a story going round among the detainees and among the Defence counsel that it was dangerous to try and prove before this Trial Chamber that somebody helped somebody, because if they didn't help anybody out, then they say that he was inhuman because he didn't help anybody out. Now, if he did happen to help somebody out, then this is a grievous circumstance because it means he had authority to do that. So it's a very dangerous point. You have to look at things black and white, in a black-and-white way, and as we all know, life is never black and white. We have direct and indirect evidence, and you'll see this from the testimony of all witnesses who said that he did indeed help them. One from Australia was heard by a Prosecutor, Mr. Niemann. He said that -- this witness said that he had saved his life, in fact. The number of people who Mladjo Radic helped in one way or another amounts to about 150. Now, why didn't he help everybody? Well, if every guard helped 150 detainees, and there were 20 to a shift, and there were never 3.000 people in Omarska camp at any one time. So if everybody had just helped 150, that's no small number, is it, and does that make matters worse? When everybody who was helped, they said he did it secretly, not through force of his own authority, but clandestinely so that other people wouldn't see. You have a detail, when he brings in bread, for example, he leaves the bread there and when he leaves, another guard takes up the bread. Is that that famous principle of authority, the term authority that prevails here? Because we're afraid of saying that people helped each other because in doing so we would recognise the command structure in the camp. And we saw that he -- when he did assist people he never assisted them pursuant to orders. He did it indirectly. Witnesses would say that he helped them as a friend, as a man. He did what he could to make their lot better. I felt the need to tell you this along with something else. You can see that the term Krkan's shift is used. Don't forget one more detail which is a very important detail. He's an active-duty policeman. He is the eldest active policeman, and he served in all the surroundings villages, Ljubija and whatever. Everybody knew him. He was an active-duty policeman, as the others were reservists or whatever. And that's why they referred to his shift as Krkan's shift because they recognised him. He recognised the people, the people recognised him. If they couldn't recognise anybody, those people are not here today. They weren't put on trial here. And finally, the most important point, or rather, it's not the most important point, but I'd like to say it nonetheless. We cannot believe everybody a priori, of course. I indicated Witness A's testimony, for which he was imprisoned, and she said on television that she was raped. When she was on television, she stated her full name and surname. Here she was a protected witness and was assigned a pseudonym. But we have ascertained that the shifts lasted -- the court ascertained that the shifts lasted 12 hours. And then he says that perhaps Hase Icic cannot remember how long the shifts were. How wouldn't he remember when he saw -- if he saw someone in the morning and saw him then again in the evening? Of course he remembers but he didn't see Mladjo Radic in the evening if he saw him at all. And shifts could not have lasted longer than 12 hours. Then we have witnesses who speak about the fact that everybody could do what he wanted over there. And don't forget that there were 20 people to a shift and very often they didn't know each other, these people who were working on the shifts together. And the shifts and the composition of those shifts was not determined by any of the accused, if anybody who turned up was just there and did his job. Now, before I go on to the question of rape I should just like to raise one basic question once again, and that is that the Trial Chamber quite simply failed to establish, and that is my main objection, which acts Radic should have undertaken and did not undertake, or rather, whether he was able to do anything. If we have that there was general anarchy reigning in the camp with everybody doing what they saw fit. So if he failed to do that, you cannot hold him responsible for what the guards committed, guards whom he never even saw from his vantage point and his shift. And I have already explained in greater detail why he's not responsible for the conditions that prevailed in the camp. And this brings me to something that I hold dearest to my heart when it concerns my client, Mr. Radic. It is least important for him what you're actually going to decide with respect to his role in Omarska. He is not proud of having been there. None of them are proud of having been there as you were able to see, nor does he want to shirk responsibility for being there. However, placing his destiny and fate before you, let me repeat that he has three sons, he has a wife. He was threatened that they would be sent to the army and then be killed. And he asked to be replaced because he saw people whom he had previously worked with being brought to Omarska. He went to Simo Drljaca, and Simo Drljaca sent him packing and said, "Do your job." So he felt that something was amiss. But that is not the essential point here. What is essential, both for him and for myself, is that we prove to this Trial Chamber that there was no rape concerned. They broke his shoulder when they arrested him. He is a permanent invalid. He suffers from diabetes; he is being given an insulin [as interpreted] today. But all that is, once again, not essential. What is essential is face, to preserve face. In a war, people fight, but people do not rape in a war. So I entreat you that you pay special attention to that part of my appeal. I should like to ask you to scrutinise very well, in minute detail, to see how it is possible for violations in the proceedings -- how to force proceedings along the lines of him being proclaimed guilty. And when I spoke of the Statute, I spoke of those four individuals and whether there was anything there or not. But Witness K, let's look at the testimony of Witness K. In 1993, she was interviewed and said no. She said to the papers no. She kept saying that the commander of Keraterm security, Dusko Sikirica, committed rape. But nobody believes her, neither the Prosecution nor the Trial Chamber. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (redacted) . But of course you, as a court of law, will be able to have access to that transcript. And suddenly in 1995, she thinks of saying something like that, of claiming it. And then these hallucinations begin. She says the morning, then she says the evening, then she says it was up there, then she says it was down here. Then she says, "Witness Vinka brought me," whereas she said that he was a good man. And she said that he said -- that he was a good man towards Muslims and Vinka is a Serb. So why would he -- would his conduct towards her have been bad if he had discriminatory intent? There is no discriminatory intent towards members of one's own ethnic group. That's quite another story. Vinka was proposed as a witness to say that she did not take her to Mladic -- to Radic. You had the whole model of Omarska camp before you. You saw that investigators beat up people throughout the day. So how could this man have raped with all these 200 people around or 200 people? You can see the video footage. She thought all this up. She conjured it all up. Because in preparing this, we were able to go through her biography to establish that she was mentally deranged, that she was taken to Court several times, that she spent her time stealing television sets, and that is why -- whereas she was brought into Court [as interpreted]. So what can I find in the space of five or six days, given those circumstances? There are one or two differences, they say. What do you mean, one or two differences? Take a look at each of her statements. There are no two statements that are the same, and that is the key point. That is why I ask you to scrutinise, to look into it carefully. Give him 200 years, sentence him to 200 years imprisonment if you like but he has to live with this. He has three sons, he has a wife who visits him. So if he did commit that act, he should be held responsible. But what if he didn't? And he was arrested because of A. And he was -- Witness K gave testimony in 1993 in the Office of the Prosecutor, and says that, no, this did not happen in Omarska. In 1995, he says to Mrs. Brenda Hollis that nobody had asked him anything along those lines. We found that from 1993. And then she said, well, that was something else again. So the Court says she was ashamed. How could she be ashamed if she says -- ashamed of having been raped by Mladjo Radic if she said that Sikirica raped her over and over again?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We say that one third of sentencing for rapes are not always in place, but we also know that out of shame, people don't report rapes. So there is no woman that has been raped and is proud of it. She always feels shame. But how come she is not ashamed because of Keraterm and suddenly, in 1995, she states that this happened to her in Omarska and that it happened once and then turns this round and round. She says it was in the morning, then she says it was in the evening, it happened like this, it happened like that. And the Trial Chamber found that her testimony was unreliable generally. There is no criminal act that I hate more than the crime of rape, believe me when I say that. That is the most atrocious crime. And if it is done with discriminatory intent, then it is even more horrendous. But we have no discriminatory intent here. Just remember all the stories that the witness said. She said it was like this, then she said it was like that, and then it was established that she had construed the whole thing. In each of Witness K's segments and parts of her testimony, there are things that were impossible. In 1995, she said -- she told Brenda Hollis that she wasn't raped. Then she said she was raped at night, then she said she was raped during the day. Then in answer to all the questions she says, "Well, I don't know, but I suppose that what I said to Ms. Hollis was right." So rape is not an act you can forget. It is not the same as whether I ate an ice cream three or four days ago. So that from the Sikirica case, and I'm saying this because this happened subsequently, the Keraterm judgement came subsequently, and we can see clearly there that nobody believed her. The Prosecution presented the arguments saying that you can believe one and not another person, but this is new. Keraterm didn't believe her. And you'll be able to see that in Sikirica plea agreement. In the document, all the details are there. And as I've already said, the testimony of Vinka Andzic is manipulated. We only asked her one thing, "Did you take this woman out or not?" She said no and that's it. And that's the whole value of her testimony. We now come to Witness AT, once again a legal question, for the second time, a legal question brought up for the second time. What does that mean? What should it mean? Does it mean that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence must be applied --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I ask you--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I ask you very kindly to attend to the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I've almost finished. I've left this to the end. Otherwise I'll be repeating myself. So with respect to Witness AT and an attempt at the witness -- at the rape of Witness J, let's look at how this has been presented. And finally, the last point is the question of the fact that Witness J tells the same story where two men are concerned. She applies it to two individuals. Rule 93 was not applied properly, once again. And finally, and that will be my conclusion, as far as the sentence is concerned, I have set it all out in writing and I think it would be superfluous for me to explain the mitigating circumstances that you will find set out in the document. Thank you for hearing me out. I wasn't going to take an hour, but you know what lawyers are. I seem to have taken longer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Weinberg de Roca would like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Weinberg de Roca would like to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Fila, you mentioned that the accused should often be tried by the local courts. And in this case, is this because the Yugoslav Penal Code rape involves permanent and lasting injury of the victim and simultaneous use of force and threat? Is this why you're suggesting that rape was not -- did not occur in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. No, heaven forbid. No. Don't underestimate my powers of reasoning, please. If he did commit rape - if, if - then you are responsible for finding him guilty. The position of Mr. Radic is that he did not commit rape. If he did, of course, you are the competent authority to judge. Now, as triers at a local level are concerned, the reason that I mention that is that the fact that the Prosecution gave up on the other 13, on trying the other 13 guards, was this: I said that if some criteria was set, then Mladjo Radic was just like these other 13, and a man named Pavlic said that he had owned up and said that he had killed a man. None of these people have said that they killed anybody or are here for having killed somebody, which is the gravest crime, of course, with rape. So my answer to you is no, no, that is not what I claimed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Also you concentrated very much on the testimony of Witness K, which you examined when the trial. But there were also other witnesses, Witness J, Witness F, Witness Susic, and Witness Cikota. You didn't mention those but only spoke about Witness K. Is there a specific reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason is that in the beginning, when I spoke about the Statute, I said that as far as I'm concerned, the fact -- what those four persons are saying, as far as I'm concerned, is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not true because that is what Radic claims. This is one thing. But if it were true, without the rape of Witness K, these are not grave violations of international law, according to my opinion. And this is the decision that you need to rule on, independently looking at it. I hope that I was clear. And this is why I did not deal with this matter. If you were to establish - and I hope that you will - that Witness K was not raped and that AT cannot be considered to be typical conduct, because that was not presented properly, would you believe that then there was an occurrence of a grave violation of international humanitarian law in relation to what those four other witnesses said independently, out of context? And this is why I wanted you to clarify Article 2 of the Statute. What these grave violations are. Because if somebody had said what the grave violations are, there must have been violations which were not of such a grave nature. This is why I skipped over this in less detail. I don't know if this answer is satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I am obliged to you for your very stimulating submissions. I would like to benefit more from your thinking than time allows. So I'll confine myself to two little areas. Now, Judge Weinberg de Roca adverted to your submissions regarding Witness K. Now, just suppose, just suppose that the Bench were inclined to agree with you that there was no rape in the case of that witness. Would that be sufficient to allow the appeal, or would we have to go a further step and to say that, as you do, the Appeals Chamber must be satisfied that no reasonable tribunal of fact could have found as the Trial Chamber did find? Would your submissions go as far as that? Would you say that not only didn't the evidence warrant the conclusion that rape occurred, but that no reasonable tribunal of fact could have so found?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to respond, Your Honour. I don't think that you will like the answer. I don't understand the term "reasonable trier." Does that mean that I need to claim now that Judge Rodrigues, Judge Riad, and Judge Wald were unreasonable triers? That would be terrible. I hope that you will not tell me that I am unreasonable, even though you have every right, because you are a Judge. I don't understand the sense of that term. I was there. We all saw Judge Rodrigues off. So can how can I look you in the eye and say you did not reach a reasonable decision -- and I know your entire curriculum vitae. I don't understand this criterion. I don't get it. But it's part of continental law. If I had written in an appeal that a judge had reached an unreasonable decision, that would be contempt of court, where I come from. So this is something that I will not say. But I will say that such a decision could not have been reached. But I will not say that this was an unreasonable decision. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please. We cannot hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand your protestations against the concept of a judge being unreasonable. Nevertheless, this concept occurs, as you well know, in the legal systems of many countries, one applies a test as to whether a reasonable trier of fact could have come to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in my book, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And I could give you examples, if I were minded to and if time allowed. But unfortunately we are prisoners of the chronometer. Now let me turn to a second area in which I need the benefit of your help.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you permit me, Your Honour, I will tell you in one sentence. What I am concerned about is the fact that it was definitely established that Witness A was not speaking the truth and that we have switching of issues here. This is what is concerning me here. Not unreasonableness, but switching of facts. While the witness who claimed in two proceedings that she was raped is not objecting. So this is the most that I can provide by way of an explanation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me see if I can benefit from your thinking in the short time that remains. So I turn to the second area of curiosity. You were talking about Mr. Radic, and you said he had the lowest possible police rank. Now I can see an argument to the effect that the rank of the accused has a certain relevance. If the charge against him is based on command responsibility, you want to show he had some authority. But would you say the argument rings as true if the charge against him is based on joint criminal enterprise?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The reason why we mentioned his low rank is that I believe that when one enters a joint criminal enterprise, enters into a joint criminal enterprise, I'm not imagining this to be like the Knights of the Round Table where we sit and we conceive of a joint criminal enterprise. This is not something that you see in a cartoon. I mean, it's something that you can accept later. But the required degree of volition and degree of intelligence, and we have findings here by psychiatrists and psychologists. This is a man who is obedient. He is not aggressive. Just see how he was described as a family person: The father of three sons, spent his whole life without advancing in his profession. He's just a merry person. So such a structure of personality to me does not fit into this type of enterprise. So this is the sense in which I referred to it. This personality type does not fit into that kind of activity. And perhaps this applies to the other two as well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Thank you very much. Now -- yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just wish to bring a particular matter to your attention, and it concerns particularly part of the submission of my learned friend with regard to confidential information, with regard to a particular witness. I think it is an irrelevant fact, may warrant redaction. Because I do recall quite, quite lucidly that, at trial, applications were made by the Defence to adduce evidence with regard to the medical record of certain witnesses and this was rejected by the Trial Chamber. And this matter in fact was not pursued. The Prosecution is deeply concerned that attempts have been made by the bar table to adduce evidence based on private conversations emanating thereof. And in the circumstances, we are requesting, in fact, that the Court consider redaction of that particular area. I didn't want to interrupt my friend because he was in full flight. But I thought the exigencies of justice demand that the witness's confidentiality is maintained and maintained resolutely in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First I would like to thank you for not interrupting me. That is very kind of you. The second thing I wanted to say is that this is not private information that we're talking about. If you look properly, you'll see that there was a meeting between the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution about the state of health of the person that we referred to. That was an inter partes meeting that we discussed. And you can find that. Ms. Hollis probably has that matter covered. And you will see. Ms. Hollis initiated this matter, not me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is there any question of confidentiality which is involved?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. There was a meeting between the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber, and you have that on this matter. This is what I mentioned. But I did not mention the actual state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That evidence is on public record, in the normal way?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it is not. No, it is not. But later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What Mr. Carmona is suggesting --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Carmona was not there. I received this information through private channels. There was a meeting where there was a question about this, and there was a Trial Chamber decision whether this witness can or cannot -- I don't want to discuss any more of it. Perhaps Mr. Carmona doesn't know all the information referring to this matter. But Ms. Hollis is still here. Perhaps she would be able to inform you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: I am indeed privy to the said applications that were made by counsel. I am -- I don't have it in my possession. But in any event, what I'm concerned about, and my friend obviously is aware of it, that this particular information would have in fact been inter partes and was not public information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Fila, what is being suggested is that the references to this incident be redacted from today's transcript. It wouldn't affect the outcome of the case, in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing against that. I just reacted to this point that it was a privately received information. No, it is not. I could not privately find out about such a meeting. This is what I wanted to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would it be possible to make the redactions?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We could redact it. But it's -- I believe it may be too late to redact it from the transcript live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would it be possible for you to redact as much as possible?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: On that note, we will take the adjournment until tomorrow at -- what time? At 9.30. 9.30 a.m. tomorrow. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of March, 2004, at 9.30 a.m.
